name: Sara Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to tech companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. So you can tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: This time of year it's pruning. I'm out in the rows by half seven with loppers and a saw, taking out the old wood so the trees fruit properly next year. We've got 60 hectares of apples and pears, and I work for the Kowalskis, who've had the orchard for three generations. In autumn it's picking season and I help run the seasonal crew, checking bins, driving the forklift to the cold store, that kind of thing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like blossom week, when the whole place goes white and smells like honey. What wears me out is pruning in the rain with cold hands, and the money, if I'm honest. I rent a small flat above the bakery in town, on my own, and I've got maybe two or three weeks saved. Rent takes nearly half my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right to me. Lots of talk, some useful bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for some things and that's that. At work I'd say the Kowalskis' weather app is the best bit of tech we've got and that's not new. Online I'd just carry on posting blossom photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, a bit. But the orchard's problems would still be there: frost in April, pickers who can't get visas, and supermarkets paying less every year. AI wasn't going to fix any of that, and it not happening doesn't fix it either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep pruning and picking and doing what I do. I'd still use the chat thing now and then, like when I asked it to help me write an email to my landlord about the damp. I'd try to get Mr Kowalski to put me through the spraying certificate so I'm worth a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Same as now, which is fine but not great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the email to your landlord. How did that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helped me say it politely instead of angrily, which I'd never manage on my own. The landlord fixed the damp in two weeks. So I'd say it's good for that kind of thing, the stuff you'd ask a friend who's good with words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the job better, in a world where nothing much changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay, mostly. And a contract that runs all year, so I'm not wondering every January whether there's enough pruning to keep me on. It's always fine in the end, but the wondering is tiring.

S0.say: I'd say AI is handy for some things and that's that. At work I'd point out the weather app is the best tech we've got and it isn't new, and I'd keep posting blossom photos online.
S0.think: I'd be a bit relieved, but the orchard's problems would still be there: frost in April, pickers who can't get visas and supermarkets paying less every year. AI not happening doesn't fix any of that.
S0.do: Keeps pruning and picking and uses the AI chat tool now and then for things like letters. Asks her employer to put her through the spraying certificate to raise her value.
S0.feel: Calm, the same as now: fine but not great.
S0.quote: It's always fine in the end, but the wondering is tiring.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is level-headed and uses AI the way she'd use a friend who's good with words. Her worries are practical: rent, short contracts and orchard risks like frost and labour shortages. She shows no strong opinions about who's to blame, just a steady wish for more security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady change. Yes, I can see that. There are already apple-picking robots in trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so we should get ready instead of moaning. At work I'd say we should watch the trials and see if the robot pickers are any good. Online I'd probably share a video and ask what other orchard people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the seasonal pickers lose out first, and then people like me. The robot pickers I've seen use a sort of vacuum tube that sucks the apple off. They're slow now, but in a few years they won't be. I'd probably keep a job running them, if I learn fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see one work on a farm like ours, because the trials are all on big flat farms with perfect rows. Once the Kowalskis or a neighbour got one that worked, I'd ask to be trained on it straight away. I'd also start saving £50 a month, cutting the gym membership I barely use anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like seeing frost on the forecast during blossom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss if the picking went to robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew, honestly. The same Bulgarian family comes back every year, and the grandmother brings us all cake on the last day. If the robots pick, there's no crew and no cake. It sounds small, but that's half the reason I like autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would decide whether the farm buys a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Kowalski, and really the bank. He'd only do it if it saved money, and he'd ask me and the foreman what we thought. I'd tell him honestly, even if it meant less work for the crew.

S1.say: It's coming, so we should get ready instead of moaning. I'd suggest we watch the trials to see if robot pickers are any good, and ask other orchard people online what they think.
S1.think: I think the seasonal pickers lose out first, then people like me. The vacuum-tube pickers are slow now but won't be for long, and I'd probably keep a job running them if I learn fast enough.
S1.do: Waits to see a picking robot work on a farm like hers, then asks to be trained on it straight away. Saves £50 a month by cancelling a gym membership she rarely uses.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like seeing frost forecast during blossom.
S1.quote: If the robots pick, there's no crew and no cake. It sounds small, but that's half the reason I like autumn.
S1.fieldNote: Sara is ready to adapt but waits for proof on a farm like hers, not a flat trial site. Her biggest emotional loss wasn't her job but the picking crew and the grandmother's cake. She'd give her boss an honest view even if it cost the crew work, which shows her practical streak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's one pruning season and two harvests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, and that's not anyone's fault in particular, it just came too fast. At work I'd say let's be sensible and see what help is going. Online I'd ask other growers what they're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be out of a job by the second harvest. And I live on my own, so there's no second wage. I'd have rent due on the first of the month and no idea where the next pay comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd move back in with my mum and dad, which I'd hate, but the flat would go straight away. I'd take whatever training is on offer, even if it's just short courses. And I'd look for any work going, the cold store, the bakery downstairs, anything, while the government sorts out what it's going to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That knot in your stomach when you get a letter you don't want to open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it be like moving back home at 27?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be lovely about it and I'd still feel like a failure. They live forty minutes away, in a town with even fewer jobs than here. I'd lose the orchard and my little bit of independence at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bakery. Do you think the bakery would still need people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. The card says robots can do almost anything. But I'd like to think people still want to buy bread from a person. I'd be betting on that because I wouldn't have anything else to bet on.

S2.say: Nobody's ready, and that's not anyone's fault in particular; it just came too fast. At work I'd say let's be sensible and see what help is going, and I'd ask other growers online what they're doing.
S2.think: I'd be out of a job by the second harvest, and I live alone, so there's no second wage. I'd have rent due on the first of the month and no idea where the next pay would come from.
S2.do: Gives up her flat and moves back in with her parents. Takes any short training on offer and looks for any work at all, from the cold store to the bakery downstairs.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with the knot in her stomach of an unwanted letter.
S2.quote: My mum would be lovely about it and I'd still feel like a failure.
S2.fieldNote: Living alone on thin savings makes the fast picture especially hard for Sara, as no second income cushions her. Her first move is to give up her flat, which she sees as losing independence. She doesn't blame anyone and holds onto a hopeful bet that people still want bread from a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like a plan you can make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. At work I'd push the Kowalskis to get on the robot trials early, so we know how they work before everyone else. Online I'd share any good training I found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me a couple of good years running the machines, and then I don't know. If AI can do almost anything by 2031, the robot minder goes too. But a couple of years is time to save something and think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd do the spraying certificate and any robot training the dealers offer. I'd save £100 a month, which means cutting a lot, maybe getting a cheaper flat or a flatmate. By year three I'd look at what's still needed, maybe going back to college for something I haven't thought of yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Like when you know the frost is coming and you've got the fans ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really take a flatmate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it, but yes. My friend Jo from school has asked twice. Two of us in the flat would save me about £300 a month, which is more than I could save any other way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you go back to college for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet, and I don't want to pretend I do. Maybe something with people, like teaching kids about growing food. I'd want to see what others were doing first.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if people start now. I'd push my employers to join the robot trials early so we understand the machines first, and share good training online.
S3.think: Five years gives me a couple of good years running the machines, and then I don't know, because the robot minder goes too. But a couple of years is time to save something and think.
S3.do: Takes the spraying certificate and any dealer robot training in year one. Saves £100 a month, partly by taking a flatmate, and by year three looks at going back to college.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, like having frost fans ready when frost is forecast.
S3.quote: I don't know yet, and I don't want to pretend I do.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Sara's steady, practical approach comes back: train on the machines early, save hard, then reassess. She would take the flatmate she has turned down twice to save £300 a month. She was honest about not knowing what she'd retrain for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That's a lot of blossom weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so let's plan it rather than panic. At work I'd talk to the Kowalskis about the future of the orchard. Online I'd probably not say much, I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. I could have a full second career in that time. But I'd also be thinking about whether I'll ever own anything, a house, a bit of land, before it all changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the spraying certificate and save what I can. Around year three or four I'd retrain properly, maybe as a teaching assistant or in something like garden design, where people still want a person to talk to. And I'd try to buy a small place before 2036, because I'd want a home before the jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little worried underneath, but it's the normal kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to stay in the orchard if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if there was a job. But if the robots prune and pick, the only job left is the Kowalskis'. And they've got a son, so it's not going to be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is buying a place realistic on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on my own, not right now. If I retrain into something better paid, or if I meet someone, maybe. I'd keep it as a goal and not beat myself up if it didn't happen.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this properly, so let's plan rather than panic. I'd talk to my employers about the orchard's future and not say much online, just get on with it.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable, long enough for a second career. But I'd be wondering whether I'll ever own anything, a house or a bit of land, before it all changes.
S4.do: Takes the spraying certificate and saves in year one, then retrains around year three or four, perhaps as a teaching assistant or in garden design. Aims to buy a small home before 2036.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with the normal kind of worry underneath.
S4.quote: If the robots prune and pick, the only job left is the Kowalskis'. And they've got a son, so it's not going to be mine.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Sara plan calmly, and her focus shifts from the job to owning a home before the change. She sees clearly that once robots do the work, the only human role left belongs to the owning family. Her plans are realistic and she doesn't oversell them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I live on my own and rent takes half my pay, so two years would put me back in my old bedroom at my mum's. What would help is some sort of payment that covers rent while people retrain, and training that's free and close by, not two hours away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the seasonal crews. They're not in your study, I suppose, but they'd lose more than any of us. Nobody asks them anything.

headlineQuote: If the robots prune and pick, the only job left is the Kowalskis'. And they've got a son, so it's not going to be mine.
portrait: Sara Olsen is a 27-year-old junior worker on a 60-hectare apple and pear orchard, pruning in winter and helping run the seasonal picking crew in autumn. She lives alone in a small rented flat above a bakery, with rent taking nearly half her pay and two or three weeks of savings. She uses AI now and then, like a friend who's good with words, and waits to see new machines work on a farm like hers before she commits. In AGI by 2028 she'd lose both her job and her flat, but with five or ten years she plans steadily: training, a flatmate, savings and eventually a different career. She blames no one and keeps her plans realistic.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because living alone on thin savings would send her back to her parents' home.
whatWouldHelp: A payment that covers rent while people retrain, and free training close to home.
